# LLDP as a MikroTik RB941-2nD (RouterOS) answers it, captured from
# 10.3.6.2 on 2026-09-17. Addresses are rewritten into the RFC 7042
# documentation range, exactly as `diag --anonymize` would; nothing
# else about the answer is changed.
#
# Two things in here are the whole point of the fixture.
#
# 1. lldpRemLocalPortNum is 0 for every neighbour. The index below is
#    <column>.<timeMark>.<localPortNum>.<remIndex>, and the middle two
#    components are zero on all four rows. Port 0 does not exist, so
#    the table says nothing at all about which local port a neighbour
#    arrived on — not a bridge-port number, not an ifIndex, nothing.
#
# 2. lldpRemChassisId has subtype 4 (macAddress) and then carries
#    SEVENTEEN BYTES OF ASCII instead of the six binary octets the
#    subtype promises — marked `text` below, and that is what those
#    bytes really are. Read literally it is a string, and a string
#    matches nothing: not the forwarding table, which is keyed by
#    addresses, and not the switch it names.
#
# Format: <oid> <int|text|hex> <value>. `text` is an OctetString whose
# bytes are the ASCII of the value; `hex` is the raw octets.

# --- lldpLocPortTable: this device's own ports ---
# subtype 3 = macAddress, and here the six octets really are six octets
1.0.8802.1.1.2.1.3.7.1.2.1 int 3

1.0.8802.1.1.2.1.3.7.1.2.3 int 3

# --- dot1dBasePortIfIndex: bridge-port -> ifIndex ---
# Five bridge ports for seven interfaces: pwr-line1 (ifIndex 5) is not
# in the bridge, so the numbering stops being the identity at port 5.
1.3.6.1.2.1.17.1.4.1.2.1 int 1

# --- dot1dTpFdbPort: where each neighbour's address actually sits ---
# Three of the four are behind ether1, one behind ether2. Every one of
# the four chassis ids above is in here — which is why the forwarding
# table can place neighbours the LLDP table refuses to.
